BILL NUMBER:  S1747

 TITLE OF BILL :
An act to amend the education law, in relation to enacting the "New
York higher education cares act"


 PURPOSE :
This bill enacts the "SUNY/CUNY Cares Act" which allows the
administrations of city and state universities and colleges,
independent and private higher education institutions to develop and
implement a program that would collect and distribute possessions left
behind by students at the end of a school year to local
not-for-profits.

 SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS :
The education law is amended by adding a new section 239-a which
authorizes the administrations of New York City and State colleges and
universities to develop and implement rules and regulations for a
program to collect and distribute student's discarded and abandoned
consumer goods to not-for-profits located in the community where the
campus is located.

 JUSTIFICATION :
At the end of each school year, college students vacate their dorms
leaving behind numerous items including, but not limited to, home
furnishings, nonperishable and canned foods, cookware, lighting
fixtures, appliances, sports equipment, clothing and electronics that
are still in good condition. The custodial staffs of the individual
colleges ultimately become responsible for disposing the bulk of the
goods left behind, with most going to the local landfill.  By
implementing a program to resell or donate items left behind, the
amount of solid waste going to the landfill would be significantly
reduced and the 'proceeds' whether monies raised or products donated,
would benefit any number of non for-profit organizations in meeting
the needs of their constituency.

Examples of successful programs include Penn State University's annual
"Trash to Treasure Sale," a campus-wide collection and sale of
student's unwanted items during the last weekend of the school year.
In 2007, this charity event raised $49,870 for the 39 human services
agencies funded by the Centre County United Way, donated approximately
four tons of food to area food banks, saved the University the cost of
disposing the abandoned items and prevented nearly 357 tons of solid
waste from becoming landfill. At Colorado University at Boulder, the
Environment Service Center designates spots on the campus where
students can leave unwanted and reusable items. Last year, all of the
items were given to Habitat for Humanity for a charity event that
raised money for local housing projects.

With 64 NYS university campuses and 23 NYC university campuses
(although not all city campuses offer residential facilities)
'recycling' programs such as those described above would provide local
not-for-profits a new resource for new or gently-used appliances,
furnishing, clothing, electronics, etc. or the funds to supplement
programs around the community.

 FISCAL IMPLICATIONS :
None.

 LEGISLATIVE HISTORY :
This bill was previously introduced.

 EFFECTIVE DATE :
Immediately.

summary: Enacts the "New York higher education cares act" to distribute student residual consumer goods from state universities and colleges to not-for-profit organizations.
